entries.value: Before any approval, legitimate pathways discussed in primary manufacturer/FDA-process materials are clinical trials and, in limited circumstances, expanded access (sometimes called compassionate use) coordinated with a treating physician and applicable FDA IND / IRB requirements.

Lilly Medical states that retatrutide is not currently FDA-approved; that Lilly is supporting single-patient expanded-access requests for individuals who meet eligibility criteria when they cannot join a trial and have exhausted available options; that availability depends on geography, supply, and case-by-case assessment; and that requests are physician-initiated. ClinicalTrials.gov lists pre-approval expanded access as NCT07629401.

High-level eligibility themes on Lilly Medical include refractory obesity (BMI ≥35 despite highest tolerated approved chronic weight-management therapy), at least two serious or life-threatening obesity-related complications under standard care, and inability to join an ongoing retatrutide (or comparable) trial. This page does not turn those criteria into an application guide or medical advice.
Grey-market / RUO vials sold online are not clinical-trial supply and are not expanded access. Catalog adjacency is not a manufacturer program.

entries.value: On 14 October 2026, nine U.S. senators (Jim Banks, Martin Heinrich, Ted Budd, Adam B. Schiff, Tom Cotton, Andy Kim, David H. McCormick, Jon Husted and Todd Young) wrote to Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas about online vendors that sell unapproved drugs and active pharmaceutical ingredients labeled “for research use only.” The letter uses “knockoff retatrutide” as its example and says: “We are concerned that ‘for research use only’ has become a dangerous loophole that undermines the FDA’s authority.” Sen. Banks’s office released the letter on 15 October 2026.

It cites America’s Poison Centers data showing “a 265% increase in poisonings related to illicit retatrutide in the first four months of 2026 compared to the last four months of 2025.” PeptideMap has not checked that figure against an America’s Poison Centers release.
The letter is a request from members of Congress to FDA. It is not a law, a regulation or an FDA action, and it does not change retatrutide’s status: retatrutide is not FDA-approved.

target_values.title: Biologic vs drug classification — FDA decision on remand (2 Oct 2026); Seventh Circuit appeal pending

entries.value: In January 2024, Lilly asked FDA to regulate retatrutide as a biological product under a Biologics License Application (BLA). FDA responded on 18 March 2024 that retatrutide is a drug, not a biological product. Lilly sued in the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana (No. 1:24-cv-01503), which sent issues about whether retatrutide is “analogous” to a protein back to FDA. On 2 October 2026, deciding those issues on remand, FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research concluded that “retatrutide is not an analogous product to a protein and is therefore not a biological product. Accordingly, an application for retatrutide would need to be submitted under section 505 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.” A redacted copy of the decision was filed in the Seventh Circuit on 8 October 2026 (No. 26-1301, Dkt. 46-2).

Lilly’s appeal in the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Seventh Circuit, Eli Lilly and Company v. Robert F. Kennedy, Jr., No. 26-1301, is from the district court’s judgment. The court heard oral argument on 24 September 2026 and ordered supplemental memoranda on appellate jurisdiction, which both sides filed on 8 October 2026 (Dkt. 45–47). In a footnote, Lilly’s memorandum says FDA’s new decision is “beyond the scope of this appeal” (Dkt. 47, n.3). As of 22 October 2026, no ruling appeared on the docket.

Educational takeaway only: under FDA’s 2 October 2026 decision, an application for retatrutide would be a section 505 drug application. Neither that classification decision nor the pending appeal is an approval decision, and an argument or a pending appeal is not a ruling.

target_values.title: Biologic vs drug classification — FDA decision on remand (2 Oct 2026); Seventh Circuit appeal pending

The court heard oral argument on 24 September 2026 and ordered supplemental memoranda on appellate jurisdiction, which both sides filed on 8 October 2026 (Dkt. 45–47). In a footnote, Lilly’s memorandum says FDA’s new decision is “beyond the scope of this appeal” (Dkt. 47, n.3). As of 22 October 2026, no ruling appeared on the docket.

old_values.question: How does retatrutide differ from tirzepatide?
old_values.answer: Retatrutide adds glucagon receptor agonism on top of GLP-1 and GIP. The glucagon component increases energy expenditure and fat oxidation beyond what dual agonists achieve.

old_values.question: Is retatrutide FDA-approved?
old_values.answer: No. Retatrutide is still not FDA-approved. Phase 3 TRIUMPH results are published, including TRIUMPH-1 in The New England Journal of Medicine (29 Sep 2026) and TRIUMPH-2 in The Lancet (29 Sep 2026). Eli Lilly has stated a planned U.S. biologics license application in Q1 2027. That filing plan is not FDA approval. PeptideMap is a research-use (RUO) comparison publisher, not a clinic or pharmacy. This is trial reporting, not medical advice and not a dose.

old_values.question: Why add glucagon if it raises blood sugar?
old_values.answer: The GLP-1 component offsets glucagon's glycemic effect, while glucagon's metabolic benefits (increased energy expenditure, hepatic fat reduction) add to the overall effect.

old_values.question: How do published TRIUMPH-1 results differ from TRIUMPH-2?
old_values.answer: TRIUMPH-1 (NCT05929066) is not TRIUMPH-2. Jastreboff and colleagues, for the TRIUMPH-1 Investigators, reported it in The New England Journal of Medicine (29 Sep 2026; DOI 10.1056/NEJMoa2604169; PMID 42814954): adults with obesity or overweight without diabetes, randomized to once-weekly retatrutide 4 mg, 9 mg, or 12 mg or placebo for 80 weeks (2,339 participants). The abstract states that, for weight-related endpoints, intercurrent events were handled by a treatment-regimen estimand. Under that analysis, mean percent change in body weight was −17.6% (4 mg), −23.7% (9 mg), and −25.0% (12 mg) versus −3.9% with placebo. Those abstract figures are the treatment-regimen result. They are not a treatment recommendation and not a head-to-head comparison with semaglutide, tirzepatide, or eloralintide. The same paper’s abstract does not print −28.3%. Lilly Medical’s table of TRIUMPH-1 outcomes, which cites that NEJM article, lists a separate efficacy estimand: percent change in body weight at 80 weeks was −19.0% (4 mg), −25.9% (9 mg), and −28.3% (12 mg) versus −2.2% with placebo. −28.3% is not the abstract primary weight result. TRIUMPH-2 remains the separate type 2 diabetes plus obesity or overweight trial; its published figures are not restated here and are not a ranking against TRIUMPH-1. PeptideMap is a research-use (RUO) comparison publisher, not a clinic or pharmacy. This is not medical advice and not a dose.

old_values.question: What did TRIUMPH-3 report for cardiovascular events?
old_values.answer: No. TRIUMPH-3 (NCT05882045) is not sourced from a peer-reviewed NEJM or Lancet cardiovascular-outcomes paper. Eli Lilly’s 23 July 2026 topline is the source. The trial enrolled adults with severe obesity (BMI ≥35 kg/m²) and established cardiovascular disease, with or without type 2 diabetes (1,949 participants; 9 mg, 12 mg, or placebo; 80 weeks). Under the efficacy estimand in that release, mean percent weight change at 80 weeks was −21.6% (9 mg) and −22.6% (12 mg) versus −3.2% with placebo. That is not the TRIUMPH-1 or TRIUMPH-2 result, and a treatment-regimen weight figure for TRIUMPH-3 was not in the release. The same release reported pre-specified in-study analyses of time to first event for pooled 9 mg and 12 mg versus placebo. MACE-5 was 44 events versus 52 (hazard ratio 0.82, 95% CI 0.55 to 1.22). MACE-3 was 27 events versus 23 (hazard ratio 1.12, 95% CI 0.64 to 1.96). Both intervals include 1. The release does not establish a reduction in cardiovascular events. It says these events occurred less frequently than anticipated in both the retatrutide and placebo arms. Urinary tract infection in that topline was 6.1% (9 mg) and 7.0% (12 mg) versus 5.3% with placebo in TRIUMPH-3. This is not medical advice and not a dose.
